title: Throwing flowers
hookLine: a week with nothing big to give, and Thérèse's answer: small sacrifices, thrown like petals
tomorrow: she's put in charge of the young nuns. how does she do it?

cards: Some weeks there's nothing impressive to give. No big donation, no free weekend, no grand gesture. Just a full calendar, a tired body, and a list of people who need things.
Thérèse knew a version of that. In Manuscript B, written for her eldest sister Marie, she says love proves itself by deeds. But she's young, enclosed and unknown.
There are no great deeds on offer inside her walls. No mission to sail to, no crowd to preach to. So what does a person give, when she has nothing big to give?

teach.b: She finds her answer in a childhood memory. As a little girl in church processions, she loved throwing flower petals toward the Blessed Sacrament as it passed. So, she writes, she can throw flowers.
That's her phrase for it. And what are the flowers?

teach.h: NOT ONE SMALL THING SLIPS BY.
teach.b: Not letting a single small sacrifice slip by: a look, a word, the smallest act, done for love.
The First Letter of John puts the same demand plainly, in the Douay-Rheims: "let us not love in word, nor in tongue, but in deed, and in truth." Thérèse just shrinks the deed down to petal size.
The laundry splash was a petal. So was the smile for the sister who grated on her. And the petals don't need to be pretty.
She writes that she'll keep throwing them and singing, even when she has to gather them among thorns. She's honest that the flowers have little worth in themselves.
What makes them count, she says, is the love that throws them.
So in a week with nothing big to give, her answer isn't: wait until you have more. It's: notice the small thing right in front of you, and give that.
One to tell a friend tonight: a child's game in a procession became her whole picture of a holy life.

how: Children in some Catholic parishes still scatter petals before the Blessed Sacrament in Corpus Christi processions, and Thérèse's image of throwing flowers is often used to describe offering small daily sacrifices.

games.q: your mom is working double shifts this month. every morning the dishwasher is full of clean dishes. what's a petal, Thérèse-style?
o: empty it before she's up, and never mention it.
empty it, then text her a photo so she knows.
wait for summer, when you can do something big.
games.why: Thérèse's flowers were small, unseen and given for love. telling her isn't wrong, but the petal is the hidden kind, and waiting for something big misses her whole point.

practice: Choose one small, unseen thing you could do tomorrow: refill what you emptied, take the worse chair, let someone else have the last word. Name what usually stops you, maybe tiredness, maybe wanting credit.
Then make the plan: when that moment comes, I'll do it, and tell nobody.

wordCard.voice: Throwing flowers. Thérèse's picture for small sacrifices nobody sees, tossed like petals, out of love.

orig.note: Latin for flower, the image Thérèse used for her small sacrifices.

carryVoice: Carry this with you: petals, the small unseen things thrown with love, not for credit. Until tomorrow.
